## Before the bench {.center}

### What you are about to measure

A strain gauge bridge outputs microvolts per unit strain. A board's ADC,
even after [S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd) characterized it, cannot resolve
microvolts on its own.

By the end of the session you will know:

- exactly how much amplifier gain a bridge measurement needs, from
  arithmetic against S1's own noise floor;
- what a load cell's static calibration has to separate — linearity,
  hysteresis, creep, zero drift — and how each is measured;
- how quarter, half and full bridge wiring trade sensitivity against what
  they cancel;
- what temperature compensation actually buys, measured rather than assumed.

### The rule of the session

::: {.callout-important}
## Derive the gain, do not guess it

A bridge signal that never leaves the noise floor is not a small
measurement — it is no measurement at all. Every gain used today is derived
from arithmetic against S1's numbers, not chosen because it looked
reasonable.
:::

## At the bench {.center}

### What you will build

Two amplifier stages — one for a standalone load cell, one for gauges bonded
to [the cantilever beam](../../hardware/beam-rig.qmd) — each verified at its
quiescent output before a sensor is connected.

::: {.smaller}
| Run(s) | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Load cell, loading + unloading (10 runs) | Linearity and hysteresis |
| Load cell, held load | Creep |
| Load cell, zero after the sequence | Zero drift |
| Beam gauges: quarter, half, full bridge | Sensitivity ratio 1 : 2 : 4 |
| Quarter vs. half bridge, two temperatures | Temperature compensation |
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## What ruins the session

Loading and unloading with a **different** mass sequence breaks the
hysteresis comparison. Interrupting the creep hold — even bumping the bench
— injects a step where there should be a smooth curve.
:::

### Then

Open [the handbook](handbook.qmd) for the full procedure, and one of the two
analysis templates — [Python](analysis-py.qmd) or [R](analysis-r.qmd).

They have the same sections and produce the same numbers. Both ship with
reference data, so you can read the whole analysis before you wire anything.

## What you should come away with {.center}

### Three sentences you should be able to defend

1. "A bare quarter-bridge signal at a representative strain is about
   $\dots$ mV, against a noise floor of $\dots$ mV from S1 — so the required
   gain, from @eq-m1-required-gain, is $\dots$."
2. "Our load cell showed $\dots\,\%$FS non-linearity and $\dots\,\%$FS
   hysteresis, and creep of $\dots\,\%$ over the hold, with the zero
   returning to within $\dots$ mV of where it started."
3. "Quarter, half and full bridge gave outputs in the ratio $\dots$, and the
   dummy-compensated half bridge's apparent strain per kelvin was $\dots$
   times smaller than the bare quarter bridge's."

If you can say those three with your own numbers in them, the session
worked.
